title: National Press Day : Landmark Supreme Court Judgments Upholding Media Freedom
case_name: Sakal Papers v. Union of India
summary: In the 2021 Pegasus case ( Manohar Lal Sharma v Union of India ) , the Supreme Court observed that surveillance will have a chilling effect on the freedom of press. The Court noted that the protection of journalistic sources is one of the basic conditions for the freedom of press.

note.Facts: Bloomberg Television Production Services India Pvt. Ltd. sought an interim injunction against Zee Entertainment to restrain publication of a news article in a defamation suit.
note.Issue: Whether a trial court may grant a pre-trial (ex-parte) injunction restraining media publication without first establishing that the material is “malicious” or “palpably false.”
note.Held: The Supreme Court cautioned that ex-parte injunctions should be granted only in exceptional cases where the defence would unquestionably fail at trial; otherwise, injunctions must follow a full trial or give the respondent a chance to be heard.
note.Principle: Pre-trial injunctions against media publications are permissible only when the plaintiff shows the content is malicious or palpably false; otherwise, courts must balance free speech with reputation and avoid stifling public debate.
note.Provisions: Not stated (the judgment relied on constitutional freedom of speech and the need to balance it with reputation and privacy).
note.Exam angle: Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution – test the limits of free speech versus defamation; ask how the “malicious or palpably false” standard functions as a threshold for granting injunctions in media-related defamation cases.

title: Gratuity Can't Be Withheld Because Of Pending Appeal Against Acquittal: Supreme Court
case_name: Delhi Development Authority v. Rajender Kumar Sharma
ratio: Gratuity of retired employees who were acquitted in a corruption case cannot be withheld merely because the State government's challenge to the acquittal is pending.
summary: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 16) held that gratuity of retired employees who were acquitted in a corruption case cannot be withheld merely because the State government's challenge to the acquittal is pending.

note.Facts: The Supreme Court on Monday (November 16) held that gratuity of retired employees who were acquitted in a corruption case cannot be withheld merely because the State government's challenge to the acquittal is pending.
note.Held: Gratuity of retired employees who were acquitted in a corruption case cannot be withheld merely because the State government's challenge to the acquittal is pending.
note.Principle: Gratuity of retired employees who were acquitted in a corruption case cannot be withheld merely because the State government's challenge to the acquittal is pending.

title: 2002 Gujarat Riots | Supreme Court Suspends Life Sentence Of Two Bilkis Bano Rape Case Convicts
summary: The Supreme Court recently suspended the life sentences of two convicts in the Bilkis Bano gangrape and murder case and granted them bail, noting that they have spent more than 17 years in incarceration and one of them is severely handicapped.

note.Facts: Two convicts in the Bilkis Bano gang-rape and murder case, Bipinchand Joshi and Pradip Modhiya, had been in custody for over 17 years, one being severely handicapped, and challenged the life sentences upheld by the Bombay High Court.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court should suspend the life sentences and grant bail pending appeal, considering the length of incarceration and the appellant’s handicap.
note.Held: The Supreme Court suspended the life sentences and granted bail on terms to be fixed by the trial court, noting the long imprisonment and severe handicap, while the appeals against conviction will be heard later.
note.Principle: A life sentence may be suspended and bail granted when the convict has spent an extended period (here, >17 years) in custody and there are substantial factual or legal issues, especially if the convict is severely disabled.
note.Provisions: IPC §§ 143, 147, 302 read with 149; §§ 376(2)(e) & ( g); § 376(2)(g) for rigorous imprisonment; Sections 201 & 218 IPC (mentioned for police/doctor acquittals); High Court judgment (May 04 2017); Supreme Court order (Oct 28 2024).
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – suspension of sentence & bail pending appeal; IPC – offences of murder, rioting, gang-rape; could be asked on the criteria for granting bail to life-sentence convicts or on the effect of prolonged incarceration on sentencing.

title: Supreme Court Awards Rs. 30 Lakhs To Man Kept In Jail For 7 Years Despite Acquittal, Recommends Law To Compensate Illegal Custody
summary: The Court noted that the Chhattisgarh authorities displayed "complete remissness" in the matter.

note.Facts: Devilal Gond was acquitted by the Chhattisgarh High Court on 20 Jan 2018, but remained in prison until 19 May 2025 due to a communication gap between jail authorities and legal-aid officials.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court should award compensation for the unlawful detention suffered after an acquittal and what legislative measure is required to prevent such occurrences.
note.Held: The Court awarded ₹30 lakhs compensation to Gond and directed all High Courts to consider directions similar to those of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, including the establishment of an Online Criminal Justice Ecosystem for timely communication of judicial orders.
note.Principle: The State is liable to compensate a person who is illegally detained after an acquittal, and a statutory framework is necessary to prescribe parameters for such compensation and to ensure prompt transmission of court orders to prison authorities.
note.Provisions: not stated (the judgment notes the absence of any legislative provision on compensation for wrongful incarceration).

title: Bhakra-Beas power dispute: Supreme Court directs Punjab and Haryana to pay Himachal Pradesh’s 13,066 MU energy arrears over 20 years
summary: Supreme Court: While adjudicating the long-standing dispute between the State of Himachal Pradesh and the States of Punjab and Haryana concerning the allocation of power generated from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas Hydro-Electric Projects, a three-Judge Bench of Surya Kant, CJ * with Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, JJ. , directed Punjab and Haryana to supply.

note.Facts: Himachal Pradesh sued Punjab, Haryana, Union of India, Rajasthan and Chandigarh before the Supreme Court under Article 131 for its share of power from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas hydro-electric projects, claiming 7.19 % entitlement. After the 2011 decree fixing the share, the parties disputed the valuation of arrears, capital-cost liability and mode of payment.
note.Issue: Whether the present proceedings can revisit matters already decided in the 27 September 2011 decree, and how the energy-arrears and capital-cost liability are to be settled.
note.Held: The Court held that the present suit is an execution proceeding; it cannot be used to reopen issues conclusively decided in the 2011 judgment. It directed Punjab and Haryana to supply the remaining 13,066 million units (after adjusting Himachal’s capital-cost liability of ₹420.77 crore) on a cash-less basis over 20 years and dismissed all pending applications.
note.Principle: Execution proceedings may not be employed to relitigate substantive rights already settled by a prior judgment; the entitlement of a successor state flows from the statutory apportionment provision (Section 78 (1), Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966).
note.Provisions: Section 78 (1), Punjab Reorganisation Act 1966; Article 131 of the Constitution; Supreme Court judgment dated 27 September 2011 (declaring 7.19 % entitlement).
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the application of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 (especially Section 78) and Article 131 in inter-state disputes, focusing on the distinction between execution and merits proceedings and the rule that a decree’s substantive findings are conclusive.

title: Past Criminal Cases Alone Can't Justify Police Surveillance: Telangana High Court Issues Guidelines For Opening, Review Of Rowdy Sheets
case_name: G. Harinath Goud v. State of Telangana & Others
summary: The Telangana High Court issued comprehensive guidelines governing opening, closure of rowdy sheets and police surveillance emphasizing that the object of surveillance is preventive and not punitive and its continued maintenance, in absence of sufficient reasons interferes with personal liberty of a person exposing him to social stigma. The court passed the order while quashing a rowdy.

note.Facts: The Telangana High Court issued guidelines on the opening, closure of rowdy sheets and police surveillance, emphasizing that surveillance is preventive, not punitive, and that its continuation without sufficient reason infringes personal liberty and causes social stigma.
note.Issue: Whether police surveillance based solely on past criminal cases, without adequate justification, can be continued without violating personal liberty.
note.Held: The Court quashed the rowdy sheet, holding that continued surveillance without sufficient reasons interferes with personal liberty and is impermissible.
note.Principle: Surveillance must be preventive, not punitive; it may not be maintained absent sufficient justification, lest it violate personal liberty and cause stigma.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure (surveillance and preventive measures) – could be asked on the permissible scope and procedural safeguards for police surveillance, focusing on the need for justification and protection of liberty.

title: Delhi HC quashes ED LOCs against non- accused in RCFL—RHFL case; Holds mere pendency of investigation insufficient to restrict travel
summary: Delhi High Court: While quashing Look Out Circulars (LOCs) opened by Enforcement Directorate (ED) against the non- accused petitioners, a Single Judge Bench of Madhu Jain, J., held that the pendency of an investigation does not, by itself, justify restricting a person’s right to travel abroad, which forms part of personal liberty under Article 21.

note.Facts: The Enforcement Directorate issued Look Out Circulars (LOCs) restricting the foreign travel of petitioners who were not accused in the RCFL—RHFL case, despite their cooperation and appearance before authorities.
note.Issue: Whether the mere pendency of an investigation justifies imposing an LOC that restricts a person’s right to travel abroad.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court quashed the LOCs, holding that investigation pendency alone cannot curtail the right to travel, which is part of personal liberty under Article 21.
note.Principle: An LOC is a coercive measure and cannot be maintained solely because an investigation is ongoing; it must be based on a person-specific satisfaction that the departure would harm India’s economic or larger public interest, and alternative safeguards (undertakings, document production, travel intimation, accessibility conditions) are sufficient.
note.Exam angle: Article 21 of the Constitution; Enforcement Directorate’s powers under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act – could be asked to frame the issue of “when can a LOC be justified despite Article 21” or to list the ingredients required for invoking the economic-interest exception.

title: Lulu International Shopping Malls Private Limited v Gorinka Pratyusha and others Etc
Seriousness of UAPA charges cannot justify a blanket bar on travel abroad: Delhi HC
summary: Delhi High Court: In two petitions challenging the orders dated 06.10.2026 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge (Special Judge), Shahdara District, Karkardooma Courts in Sessions Case 163/2020 and Sessions Case 354/2022, whereby the petitioner’s applications to travel to the United Kingdom (UK) from 02.11.2026 to 01.12.2026 were rejected, a Single Judge Bench of Amit Bansal,.

note.Facts: The petitioner, an accused on bail in two cases involving UAPA offences, sought permission to travel to the UK from 02-11-2026 to 01-12-2026 for in-person PhD supervisory meetings and to present a paper at a conference; her passport was lodged with the trial court and the travel application was rejected on the ground of serious UAPA charges.
note.Issue: Whether an accused charged with serious offences under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967 can be barred from travelling abroad in a blanket manner despite being on bail.
note.Held: The Delhi High Court allowed the petitions and permitted the petitioner to travel, subject to specific safeguards, holding that the seriousness of UAPA charges does not automatically curtail the right to travel abroad.
note.Principle: The right to travel abroad, a facet of Article 21, cannot be denied on a blanket basis merely because the accused faces serious UAPA charges; the restriction must be proportionate and consider the individual’s bail record, purpose of travel, and safeguards.
note.Provisions: Article 21 Constitution of India; Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967 (Sections 13, 16, 17, 18); Penal Code, 1860; Arms Act, 1959; Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984; Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248.
note.Exam angle: Test on Article 21 (right to travel) vis-à-vis UAPA offences – could be asked to frame the issue of whether the seriousness of charges under UAPA justifies a blanket travel ban, and to enumerate the ingredients of a proportional restriction (bail status, purpose of travel, safeguards).

title: Mere Mention Of Name Without Evidence Of Role In Criminal Conspiracy Not Enough For Trial: MP High Court Quashes FIR Against Law Student
ratio: Mere reference to a person's name, without disclosure of any particular conduct or material indicating his participation in an allegedly criminal conspiracy…
summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court judgment in KSY v. State of MP. The ruling: Mere reference to a person's name, without disclosure of any particular conduct or material indicating his participation in an allegedly criminal conspiracy….

note.Facts: A law student’s name was mentioned in an FIR alleging participation in a criminal conspiracy, but the FIR contained no specific conduct or material linking him to the alleged conspiracy.
note.Issue: Whether a mere mention of a person’s name, without any disclosed act or evidence of participation, is sufficient to sustain an FIR and subject the person to criminal trial.
note.Held: The Madhya Pradesh High Court quashed the FIR, holding that such a bare reference to a name does not justify proceeding to trial.
note.Principle: A name alone, absent any allegation of conduct or material evidence of involvement, cannot be the basis for a criminal trial.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – validity of FIR; could be asked to frame the issue of “requirements for a cognizable FIR” or to list the essential ingredients that must be disclosed to sustain an FIR.

title: Third Party Claiming Ownership Or Possession Doesn't Automatically Become Necessary Party In Eviction Suit: Allahabad High Court
case_name: Smt Chandri Devi and another v. Smt
ratio: A third party asserting an independent claim of ownership, tenancy or possession over premises forming the subject matter of a pending Small Causes Court suit…
summary: The Allahabad High Court has held that a third party asserting an independent claim of ownership, tenancy or possession over premises forming the subject matter of a pending Small Causes Court suit cannot seek impleadment merely because a decree in the suit may affect the rights so asserted. The position is no different, it held, where the claim rests on a tenancy said to have been created.

note.Facts: A third party asserted an independent claim of ownership, tenancy or possession over premises that were the subject of a pending Small Causes Court suit.
note.Issue: Whether such a third party can be impleaded in the eviction suit merely because the decree may affect his asserted rights.
note.Held: The court held that the third party cannot be impleaded on that basis.
note.Principle: A third party claiming ownership, tenancy or possession does not automatically become a necessary party in an eviction suit simply because the decree may affect the rights he asserts.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the procedural law governing impleadment in eviction proceedings (e.g., CPC provisions on parties), focusing on the requirement of necessity versus mere interest.
